newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Mission Control says Mir oxygen system repaired.
newsitem.headline: Mission Control says Mir oxygen system repaired.

text.p: Cosmonauts aboard Russia's troubled Mir space station have managed to repair its faulty Elektron oxygen generating system but have not started it yet, a Mission Control official said on Thursday.

Viktor Blagov, deputy flight director at the Mission Control centre just outside Moscow, told reporters that new commander Anatoly Solovyov and engineer Pavel Vinogradov had solved the problem and hoped to start it working in the next few days.
He did not specify which of the station's two Elektron systems had been repaired and he did not elaborate on what had caused the problem.
The Mir crew, wrestling with a series of problems on the ageing space station, has been relying on a 70-day supply of oxygen "candles" since early August.
Earlier this week space officials said new parts from Earth would probably be needed to repair the main Elektron oxygen generating system in the Kvant-1 module.
A plan to run an extension cord to the back-up Elektron in Kvant-2, which is turned off to save energy, has also failed because the the crew did not have the right cable.
NASA, which has astronaut Michael Foale on Mir, said the cosmonauts had been trying to unclog what appeared to be a blockage in the piping of the Elektron in Kvant-1.
It said the cosmonauts had placed a tube from a discarded cooling garment inside the piping and filled it with water and aspirin to try to dissolve the clog.
NASA did not say the unblocking had been successful, but said the Elektron in Kvant-1 was still not operating.
A swift resolution of the oxygen system's faults would give the three-man crew a welcome boost before other vital repairs they must carry out in the coming weeks.
On Friday the crew will fly in a Soyuz spacecraft to take photographs of the Spektr's damaged exterior.
On August 20 Solovyov and Vinogradov will don spacesuits inside Mir and open the hatch to the dark, airless Spektr module to reconnect solar panels damaged in a June 25 collision with a supply ship.

Blagov said repressurising Spektr would be the main problem facing Solovyov and Vinogradov. "Nobody has ever done such a job," he said, adding that they might find not one but two or even three holes in the module.
"We do not know for sure how many holes there are. We know that Progress hit Spektr twice (during the collision)," he said.
Earlier on Thursday the old crew members, Commander Vasily Tsibliyev and flight engineer Alexander Lazutkin, returned safely to earth after six months on Mir.
Blagov said that they would be questioned about the June 25 collision and other accidents that occurred during their time on the 11-year-old space station.
Blagov said a Progress supply ship, undocked from Mir on August 6 to make room for the arrival of the relief crew, would redock on Sunday.

He said Progress, which contains 200 kg of fuel as well as waste accumulated by the crew over the past month, would be used for the orientation of Mir. Progress is expected to be dumped into the Pacific Ocean in early October, Blagov said.

Water reserves on Mir will last until October, Blagov said, adding that additional supplies would be delivered by the U.S. space shuttle in late September and by the next Progress craft due in early October.
